analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to; with 24 Senate backers but no Republican support, no hearing, vote, or floor action ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required any employer with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (about seven workdays) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or preventive care, to care for a sick child, parent, or spouse, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. It was introduced by Senator Edward Kennedy in May 2009 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who have no paid sick time. The bill's own findings state that nearly half of American workers lacked paid sick time for themselves or family care, including 79 percent of families in the lowest-earning quartile [S3]. It also protects workers from being fired or disciplined for using the time, creates Labor Department enforcement and the right to sue employers who violate it, and gives covered workers a route to paid time for court dates, relocation, or counseling related to domestic violence or sexual assault [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Workers at employers with 15 or more employees would earn one hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own medical needs, preventive care, or caring for a child, parent, or spouse.
The time can also be used to seek medical care, relocate, obtain counseling, or take legal action after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, with confidential documentation rules.

The bill bars employers from interfering with or retaliating against workers who use the time, including counting it against no-fault attendance policies, and authorizes Labor Department enforcement and private lawsuits with damages and attorney's fees.
The bill's findings state that 79 percent of families in the lowest-earning quartile lacked any paid sick time, so the mandate falls where the need is greatest.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would pay wages for up to 56 hours of leave per worker per year plus notice, recordkeeping, and certification paperwork. Employers already offering an equivalent paid-leave policy would be exempt from providing additional leave, and employers with fewer than 15 employees would not be covered at all [S2].

drawbacks.text: Covered employers would bear the direct cost of paying wages for up to seven days of leave per employee per year, plus administrative burdens of posting notices, tracking accruals, and handling medical certifications, which fell on employers at a time of high unemployment.

Employers may require a health care provider's certification only for absences longer than three consecutive workdays, and workers must give seven days' advance notice for foreseeable leave, creating compliance friction for both sides.

The mandate excludes employers with fewer than 15 employees, so many of the lowest-wage workers would remain uncovered, and accrued but unused sick time does not have to be paid out when a worker leaves the job.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is a guaranteed paid safety net that the bill's findings note was absent in the United States, then one of only three of 22 comparable economies with no short-term paid sick leave [S3]. The cost is real but bounded: capped at 56 hours per worker per year, with exemptions for small employers and businesses that already offer equivalent leave, so the burden concentrates on low-wage employers who previously offered nothing. It is a fairly conventional mandate design; the honest objection is that it shifts wage costs onto employers of 15 or more, and those costs are typically passed on through prices or reduced hours.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced in May 2009, and the committee never held a markup or vote, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on May 21, 2009; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Twenty-four senators cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats plus the chamber's sole Independent; no Republican cosponsored it.
The action history shows no hearing, committee vote, or floor action after the referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2011 without the bill advancing.
The bill's findings stated that nearly half of American workers lacked paid sick time and that the United States was one of only three of 22 comparable economies with no short-term paid sick leave.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who do not provide paid sick leave came out ahead: the cost of a nationwide mandate for workers at firms with 15 or more employees never materialized. Workers without paid sick days, disproportionately low-wage workers and caregivers, gained nothing.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 21, 2009 and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: 40 Senate Republicans, none of whom cosponsored

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed federal paid-sick-leave mandates during this period, arguing they raised labor costs for employers.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never moved the bill either.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and other low-wage employers with 15 or more workers
industries.note: These employers would have had to pay wages for up to 56 hours of sick leave per worker per year, and they employ the largest share of workers who currently lack any paid sick time. Their cost of compliance is the bill's public benefit.

industries.industry: Employers that already offer equivalent paid leave
industries.note: The bill exempts any employer whose existing paid-leave policy meets or exceeds its requirements, so generous employers face no new obligation and gain no new cost. Their position is locked in rather than improved.

These employers are exempt from the mandate and avoid the cost, but their employees would have remained uncovered, so the smallest workplaces gain relative to larger competitors while their workers get nothing.
